newsitem.title: USA: American Bar Assoc. to mull doctor-assisted suicide.
newsitem.headline: American Bar Assoc. to mull doctor-assisted suicide.

text.p: Now that the Supreme Court has opened the door to state authority over doctor-assisted suicide, the nation's most powerful legal group will decide whether to take a stand on controversial legislation.
At issue is whether the American Bar Association will throw its legal and political clout behind laws that either ban or allow a doctor to help a terminally ill individual commit suicide.
The ABA's annual meeting begins Thursday in San Francisco and its policy making body will vote on resolutions, including two pertaining to doctor-assisted suicide, on Aug. 5 and 6.

More than 20,000 people -- about 12,000 of whom are ABA members -- are expected to attend this year's meeting. There will be some 2,500 individual sessions and events including speeches by Supreme Court Associate Justices Sandra Day O'Connor and Anthony Kennedy; Whitewater independent prosecutor Kennth Starr and Michael Tigar, lead attorney for Terry Nichols in the Oklahoma City bombing case.
The ABA vote on doctor-assisted suicide comes shortly after the Supreme Court ruled in June that states have the right to pass laws concerning the practice and can act to ban it entirely.

It also comes as Oregon residents gear up for a November referendum challenging a 1994 initiative that allows doctor-assisted suicides. Oregon is the only state to have passed such a proposal, however the law has been on hold because of litigation.
In considering the issue, the ABA will vote on a resolution by the Beverly Hills Bar Association that proposes the national group support legislation to legalise doctor-assisted suicide.

Bert Tigerman, executive director of the Beverly Hills Bar, told Reuters that although the ABA previously defeated a similar proposal, he was more optimistic now because of the Supreme Court ruling on state authority over the issue.
He said if the group does pass the resolution, "It would certainly permit the ABA to assist and support efforts in state legislatures to draft and formulate appropriate legislation."
"It would also give considerable publicity to the act of the largest national profesional organisation," he said.
The ABA will also consider a counter proposal by its own Commission on Legal Problems of the Elderly and its Commission on Mental and Physical Disability Law.

The two commissions suggest that the ABA recommend that states and terrorities refrain from considering doctor-assisted suicide legislation "unless and until" further research confirms appropriate care and legal protections are available to terminally ill people.
